_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 11 Networks Around Us. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: the hardware (with the home router), the networked hardware around the classroom, the services, the advantages, what a network costs. The school network diagram is drawn here, in the engine's idiom, because the lesson keeps its network inside a closure; the laptop and the tablet in it are the lesson kit's own figures (ART.figure).
title: Networks Around Us
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Identify networked hardware in a familiar environment, including the school and home.
Identify services that are available on familiar networks, including digital files, printed documents and the World Wide Web.
Understand the advantages and disadvantages of a network.

beats.say: Every cable in your school goes to one box in a cupboard.
That box is a switch. It joins them all up into one network.
A school network is hardware you can point at.
The switch is the box every cable in the building comes to.
The server is a computer with no screen. It stores everyone's files.
An access point sits on the ceiling. The wi-fi comes from there.
Laptops, tablets, the printer and the whiteboard all join through them.
At home you have a router. It does the switch's job.
Look around your classroom and count what is on the network.

at.count: count what is on the network

beats.say: The computers, of course. And the interactive smartboard at the front.
That is the big screen the teacher writes on. It is on the network like any computer.
By the door is the multifunction device. One machine prints, scans and copies.
Everybody shares it, instead of three machines in three rooms.

scenes.heading: What being joined lets you do

beats.say: Being on the network gives you services: things you can do because you are connected.
Digital files. Save your work on the server and open it on any device in school.

at.save: Save your work on the server

beats.say: Printed documents. Press print on a tablet, and the school printer prints it.
The World Wide Web. Pages stored on computers all over the world.
Email and video calls too: messages and faces across the network.
A network is mostly good. Think what it gives you.
Everyone can share files. Everyone can share one printer.
Every laptop and tablet can reach the World Wide Web.
Two classes can work on one document at the same time.
It keeps a backup: a second copy, so a broken computer loses nothing.
A network costs you things too. It is good to know both sides.
When the network is down, nobody can save and nobody can print.
Cables, switches and servers cost money. Somebody has to look after them.
A file you share can be seen by people you did not mean.
It can share a computer virus: a program that copies itself and does harm.
When it stops, everybody stops at once, not just one person.
A network is hardware: a switch, a server and access points.
Being on it gives you services: files, printing and the World Wide Web.
It has advantages and disadvantages. Knowing both is understanding a network.
